causes.text: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 drug Wegovy a new indication on March 8 2024 to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke in obese or overweight adults with cardiovascular disease. The approval made Wegovy the first weight-loss medication proven to lower life-threatening cardiovascular events, underscoring the multi-billion-dollar potential of GLP-1 therapies.

source_info.title: FDA approves Wegovy to reduce risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke

effects.text: Merck signed a licensing agreement with China's Hansoh Pharmaceutical on December 18 2024 for HS-10535, an investigational oral GLP-1 agonist to treat obesity, agreeing to pay $112 million upfront and up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments. The experimental pill targets the same GLP-1 pathway as injectable drugs from Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly and is intended to diversify Merck's metabolic pipeline.

source_info.title: Merck signs up to $2 billion deal for Hansoh's oral weight-loss drug

causal_reasoning_chain.description: The FDA's cardiovascular approval for Wegovy validated GLP-1 agonists as therapies that could not only deliver significant weight loss but also reduce major adverse cardiovascular events. This landmark endorsement underscored the enormous commercial potential of the class and signalled that payers might support broader use.

Analysts predicted that oral GLP-1 formulations would expand the market beyond injectables and that companies without a metabolic franchise risked missing a rapidly growing opportunity. Merck, lacking a presence in obesity treatments, identified the need to secure a competitive GLP-1 asset to stay relevant.

On December 18 2024, Merck licensed Hansoh's oral GLP-1 candidate HS-10535, agreeing to pay $112 million upfront and up to $1.9 billion in milestones. Investors interpreted the move as a catch-up play; Merck's stock rose roughly 0.8 % in pre-market trading as the market anticipated the company's entry into the lucrative obesity segment.

rationale: The FDA's cardiovascular indication for Wegovy showcased the full therapeutic value of GLP-1 agonists and catalysed a rush to develop competing drugs.  To avoid being sidelined in a booming market, Merck quickly partnered with Hansoh to secure an oral GLP-1 candidate and signal its intent to compete.
counterfactual_analysis: If Wegovy had not demonstrated cardiovascular benefits, the obesity drug market might have grown more slowly and Merck could have delayed or avoided licensing an oral GLP-1 therapy.  Without the benchmark set by Wegovy, investors may have been less enthusiastic about Merck's entry into the space.

adversarial_confounders.text: Eli Lilly's progress with its own oral GLP-1 agonist orforglipron also increased competitive pressure on late entrants.
adversarial_confounders.impact: Lilly's pipeline advances could have influenced Merck's decision independently of Wegovy's cardiovascular approval.

details.commentary: Wegovy's landmark cardiovascular label expansion showed that GLP-1 drugs could become a standard treatment for both weight loss and heart risk, raising the threat that rivals would dominate this new paradigm. Merck's decision to license Hansoh's oral GLP-1 candidate was a strategic move to counter that threat and secure a foothold in a market increasingly controlled by a few powerful players.

details.pestel_factor: Social/Economic - Rising obesity burden and healthcare costs
details.commentary: Rising obesity rates and the enormous healthcare costs of cardiovascular disease created strong social and economic pressure to adopt effective weight loss therapies. Wegovy's approval as a cardioprotective drug highlighted how regulators and payers might reward GLP-1 medicines, making it more attractive for Merck to invest heavily in a competing oral option.

Each new piece of clinical and regulatory validation for GLP-1 therapies draws more investment into the class, broadening pipelines and reinforcing the belief that this market will be huge. Merck's licensing deal feeds that cycle by adding another candidate to the race, which in turn encourages further R and D spending and partnership activity around obesity drugs.
